title: The Shoebox of Letters
text:
My grandmother kept a shoebox of letters beneath her bed, each one tied with faded ribbon. For decades she refused to open it in front of anyone, and the family came to regard it as a sort of household relic. When she finally let me read a few pages, I discovered that the letters were not romantic at all but a meticulous record of ordinary, unglamorous wartime life.

What struck me most was her restraint: she wrote about bread queues and missing neighbours without a trace of self-pity. Reading them, I understood that memoir is less about recollection than about choosing which details deserve to survive. I have since come to think of that box as her own quiet act of authorship.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what did the grandmother keep beneath her bed?
options: A collection of letters tied with ribbon
A diary written during the war

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what did the letters describe?
What can be inferred about the grandmother's attitude toward her past?
options: She regarded it as private and was reluctant to share it
She was ashamed of her wartime experiences and wanted them forgotten
She wanted her family to publish the letters
She had forgotten the contents of the letters entirely

questions.text: What does the narrator imply about the nature of memoir?
options: It involves selecting which details are worth preserving
It must record every event in chronological order
It is mainly a record of romantic experiences
It should avoid personal emotions altogether

vocabulary.definition: an object kept because of its link to the past
showing great attention to small details
the ability to control one's emotions or behaviour

paragraph_translations: Moja babcia trzymała pudełko z listami pod łóżkiem, każdy związany wyblakłą wstążką. Przez dziesiątki lat nie chciała go otworzyć przy nikim, a rodzina zaczęła traktować je jak domową relikwię. Kiedy wreszcie pozwoliła mi przeczytać kilka stron, odkryłam, że listy wcale nie były romantyczne, lecz drobiazgowym zapisem zwyczajnego, niewyszukanego życia w czasie wojny.

Najbardziej uderzyła mnie jej powściągliwość: pisała o kolejkach po chleb i zaginionych sąsiadach, nie okazując ani śladu użalania się nad sobą. Czytając je, zrozumiałam, że wspomnienia dotyczą mniej przypominania sobie, a bardziej wyboru szczegółów wartych przetrwania. Dziś myślę o tym pudełku jako o jej cichym akcie autorstwa.
